title: Optics
lines: USAT optics questions cover reflection, refraction and total internal reflection, the lens and mirror formula, optical instruments, and the wave ideas of interference, diffraction and polarisation. Learn the formulas with their sign conventions, and know the image formed by a convex lens for each object position.
## Reflection
- Laws: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, and the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in one plane.
- A plane mirror forms a virtual, upright, same-sized image as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. Turning the mirror through θ turns the reflected ray through 2θ.
- Spherical mirrors: focal length f = R/2. A concave mirror converges light; a convex mirror always forms a virtual, upright, smaller image, giving a wide field of view.
## Refraction
- Snell's law: n = sin i / sin r, where n is the refractive index of the second medium relative to the first.
- n = c/v: light slows down in a denser medium. Its frequency stays the same, so its wavelength shortens to λ/n.
- Real and apparent depth: n = real depth / apparent depth, so a pool looks shallower than it is.
- Total internal reflection happens when light goes from a denser to a less dense medium at an angle greater than the critical angle C, where sin C = 1/n.
- Uses of total internal reflection: optical fibres (core of higher n than the cladding), prism periscopes and binoculars, the sparkle of diamond.
- Dispersion: a prism splits white light because n is slightly larger for violet than for red, so violet is deviated most.
> Example 1. Glass has refractive index 1.5. Find the speed of light in it and its critical angle (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s).
## Lenses

Pakistani textbooks use the real-is-positive convention: 1/f = 1/p + 1/q, where p is the object distance and q the image distance. Real distances are positive and virtual ones negative; a convex lens has positive f and a concave lens negative f. Magnification m = q/p (size of image ÷ size of object).
| Object for a convex lens | Image
| Beyond 2F | real, inverted, smaller, between F and 2F
| At 2F | real, inverted, same size, at 2F
| Between F and 2F | real, inverted, larger, beyond 2F
| At F | at infinity
| Inside F | virtual, upright, larger (magnifying glass)
- A concave lens always forms a virtual, upright, smaller image.
- Power P = 1/f with f in metres, in dioptres (D). Thin lenses in contact: P = P₁ + P₂.
> Example 2. An object stands 30 cm from a convex lens of focal length 10 cm. Locate the image.
> 1/q = 1/10 − 1/30 = 2/30, so q = 15 cm (positive, real). m = 15 ÷ 30 = 0.5: inverted and half size, matching the "beyond 2F" row.
## Optical instruments
- Simple microscope (magnifying glass), image at the near point: M = 1 + d/f, with d ≈ 25 cm.
- Compound microscope: a short-focus objective and eyepiece; the total magnification is the product of the two.
- Astronomical telescope in normal adjustment: M = f(o)/f(e) and length L = f(o) + f(e). It needs a long-focus objective and a short-focus eyepiece.
- Resolving power improves with a wider aperture and a shorter wavelength.
## Interference
- Interference needs coherent sources: the same frequency and a constant phase difference.
- Constructive (bright) when the path difference is nλ; destructive (dark) when it is (n + ½)λ.
- Young's double slit: fringe spacing Δy = λL/d, where d is the slit separation and L the distance to the screen.
- Thin films (soap bubbles, oil on water) show colours by interference between light reflected from the two surfaces.
> Example 3. In Young's experiment λ = 600 nm, the slits are 0.5 mm apart and the screen is 1 m away. Find the fringe spacing.
## Diffraction
- Diffraction is the spreading of waves through a gap or round an edge; it is most noticeable when the gap is about the size of the wavelength.
- Single slit: the central maximum is the widest and brightest; a narrower slit gives a wider pattern.
- Diffraction grating: d sin θ = nλ, where d = 1/N for N lines per metre.
- X-ray diffraction by crystals obeys Bragg's law 2d sin θ = nλ, with θ measured from the atomic planes.
> Example 4. Light of 600 nm falls on a grating with 5,000 lines per cm. Find sin θ for the first order and the highest order seen.
> d = 1 ÷ 500,000 m = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m. sin θ₁ = λ/d = 0.3. Orders need sin θ ≤ 1: n ≤ d/λ = 3.3, so the highest order is 3.
## Polarisation
- Only transverse waves can be polarised; this proves light is transverse.
- Unpolarised light through one polaroid loses half its intensity. Malus's law for a second polaroid: I = I₀ cos² θ; crossed polaroids (90°) let nothing through.
- Reflected light is completely polarised at the Brewster angle, where tan θ = n.
- Uses: glare-cutting sunglasses, LCD screens, stress analysis.
! Convert lines per cm to lines per metre before finding d: 5,000 per cm is 500,000 per m.
! Light entering glass keeps its frequency; only its speed and wavelength change.
! Total internal reflection is impossible when light passes from air into glass, whatever the angle.
## Quick check
- Focal length of a mirror of radius 40 cm? (20 cm)
- Fringe spacing when the slits are moved closer together? (wider)
- Lens of power −2 D: type and focal length? (concave, −50 cm)
- Which colour is deviated most by a prism? (violet)
- Telescope with f(o) = 100 cm and f(e) = 5 cm: magnifying power? (20)
